author: "Florian Richter"

This post grew out of my diploma thesis in Quantum Information, which
I wrote in Hannover in 2010. The thesis was about quantum memory
channels, and in particular about how deep their memory runs. Somewhere
inside that work a smaller, self-contained question fell out, one I
have wanted to retell ever since: how finely can you divide the most
destructive process there is?

The original is written for examiners, not for curious readers. The
arrival of large language models finally removed my last excuse. I
could not resist the temptation to rewrite the thing with agentic
support, trading the terse notation of a thesis for pictures, worked
examples, and a slower pace, so that a motivated undergraduate can
follow every step.

The heart of the post is that dividing question and its answer in the
full quantum world, a result I published years ago and that the post
reaches by the end of the quantum part. I could have stopped there.

Instead the post keeps going, into a small and well-behaved corner of
the quantum world called the Clifford channels. This last step is a
bonus, a side result I never published, and it earns its place for one
reason: it is beautiful. Restricting to Clifford channels turns the
whole problem into simple, concrete group theory, a handful of finite
states and the permutations that shuffle them, something you can work
through by hand. The reward is that even this tiny corner reaches, in
prime dimensions, asymptotically the same complexity as the full
quantum machinery. Watching a question about a physical process turn
into a question about lines over a finite field is the part I still
find surprising.

Enjoy your read :)
